overview: Verbal reasoning measures how well you work with words: understanding meaning, spotting links between words, and rearranging letters into something useful. In IQ tests it appears as unscrambling, opposites, synonyms and odd-one-out questions, usually with a tight time limit per item.

strategy.b: Read the full instruction once before looking at the options. Many lost marks come from answering a different question, such as choosing a synonym when the task asked for an opposite.
Break long strings into familiar pieces such as 'ing', 'tion' or 'pre'. Your mind recognises chunks far faster than single letters, which saves seconds on every item.
Do not stop at the first option that looks plausible. Check all four against the rule, then choose the one that fits every part of it.
Give each short item a fixed budget of around 20 to 30 seconds. If you are stuck, make your best guess and move on, because one hard item should not cost you three easy ones.

fig.title: Unscrambling in four steps
fig.note: Work from familiar chunks outward, then test the word against the clue.

drills.name: Unscramble
drills.how: You are given jumbled letters and must find the one real word they spell. Start by spotting common beginnings and endings such as 'st', 'ch', 'ing' or 'er', then build the middle around them.
drills.tip: Say the letters aloud in small groups, since the sound of a word often reveals it faster than its spelling.
drills.mistake: Trying arrangements at random wastes time and tires you out. Fix it by testing only the letter patterns that real English words use.

ex.q: Which word can be made from the letters E, P, L, N, A, T, using each one once?
ex.why: PLANET uses all six letters exactly once, and it starts with the common 'PL' and ends with 'ET'. The other options are not real words.

drills.name: Opposites
drills.how: You are given a word and must choose the option with the opposite meaning. Decide first what the word means, then look for the option that sits at the far end of the same scale rather than one that is merely related.
drills.tip: Place the given word at one end of a scale, such as hot and cold, before you read the options.
drills.mistake: Choosing a related word, such as 'cool' for 'warm', instead of its true reverse. Fix it by asking which option is furthest from the given word on the same scale.

ex.q: Which word is the opposite of ANCIENT?
ex.why: Ancient means very old, so its reverse is recent or modern. Old, historic and former all point toward the past rather than away from it.

drills.name: Same meaning
drills.how: You are given a word and must find the option that means the same thing. Read the word inside a short phrase to fix its sense, then keep the option that fits the phrase without changing its meaning.
drills.tip: Swap each option into the phrase, and the one that keeps the sentence natural is usually the match.
drills.mistake: Picking a word from the same topic but with a different meaning, such as 'quick' for 'brief'. Fix it by checking that the two words can swap in several sentences without changing the sense.

ex.q: Which word means the same as CONCEAL?
ex.why: To conceal something is to keep it out of sight. Reveal, expose and display all mean the reverse, making something visible.

drills.name: Odd one out
drills.how: You are given four words and must find the one that does not belong. Look for a category or link that three of them share, then check whether the fourth fits that link.
drills.tip: Name the category in one or two words, such as 'fruits' or 'birds', before you look at the options.
drills.mistake: Fixating on a minor detail, such as word length, when the group clearly shares a theme. Fix it by searching for the broadest shared category first.

ex.q: Which word does not belong: Apple, Pear, Carrot, Plum?
ex.why: Apple, pear and plum are all fruits that grow on trees, while carrot is a root vegetable. Naming the category first makes the odd one stand out.

drills.name: Long unscramble
drills.how: You are given a long jumbled word and must find the correct word from a set of options. Split the letters into likely pieces, then build from the start and end inward, checking the letter count as you go.
drills.tip: Count the letters first, since a correct answer must use exactly the same letters, no more and no fewer.
drills.mistake: Working left to right one letter at a time, which stalls on long strings. Fix it by locking in familiar chunks first and then assembling them.

ex.q: Which word can be made using all eight letters D, I, S, C, O, V, E, R once each?
ex.why: Count the letters: DISCOVER has eight, matching the list exactly. DISCOVERY needs a Y, which is not in the set, so it cannot be formed.

levels: Level 1: unscramble short, common words of four to five letters with clear patterns.
Level 2: unscramble six-letter words and pick opposites of everyday adjectives.
Level 3: match synonyms for common verbs and spot the odd one out in mixed categories.
Level 4: unscramble seven- to eight-letter words and match less familiar synonyms.
Level 5: solve long unscrambles that need you to find the right word among close look-alike options.
Level 6: combine every skill under time pressure, with subtle opposites and multi-word rearrangements.
routine: Day 1: spend 5 minutes unscrambling 10 common four- to five-letter words.
Day 2: do 10 opposites, saying each pair aloud as you match it.
Day 3: match 10 synonyms, testing each option inside a sentence.
Day 4: find the odd one out in 10 groups, naming the category before you look.
Day 5: take a timed mixed set of 15 items, then review every wrong answer.
